grades.quote: The RISC-V CPU raises a page-fault exception when a virtual address is used that has no mapping in the page table, or has a mapping whose PTE_V flag is clear, or a mapping whose permission bits (PTE_R, PTE_W, PTE_X, PTE_U) forbid the operation being attempted.
grades.reason: Lists the RISC-V page-fault causes (no mapping, PTE_V clear, or PTE_R/W/X/U permission bits forbidding the access). Says scause gives the fault type (load, store or instruction) and stval gives the faulting address. That tells you what to inspect, but it never says scause separates a permission fault from a missing mapping. You still have to examine the PTE.
Covers TLB hierarchy, TLB pressure and the software/hardware TLB-loading interface. It says nothing about telling a permission fault from a missing mapping.

grades.quote: If the processor generates an illegal address, the MMU interrupts the processor, transferring control to the operating system. This interrupt is known as a _page fault_ .
grades.reason: Gives a generic conceptual background. A page fault happens when an address has no translation (a blank entry), and entries can also be legal only for certain access types such as read but not write. This separates the two fault causes in concept, but it gives no way to tell them apart in practice and names no ISA.

grades.quote: Check the page table entry’s valid bit. If it is 0, then there is no page frame holding the page in question. Interrupt the processor with a page fault.
grades.reason: Describes the IA-32 walk. A page fault is raised when the PTE valid bit is 0 (no page frame, so a missing mapping). A page fault is also signalled on a permission violation at either level. This gives the two causes, but it never says how to tell them apart, such as with an error code.
